title: Wildfire help — leave safely, find support, rebuild
description: A calm, source-bound path for evacuation, smoke, safe return, immediate help, and rebuilding after wildfire.

care.title: You are seen. Your life matters more than belongings.
care.message: People beyond the fire line see what is happening and care. This page turns that care into a few practical steps and verified official doors. It is not monitored and cannot send help.
care.next_step: You do not need to finish this guide. Choose the next safe step, then go.

boundary.live_status: This is a static guide. It does not know where the fire is, which roads are open, whether a shelter has space, or whether return is permitted.
boundary.authority: Current instructions from local fire, police, emergency management, public health, and evacuation authorities override this guide.
boundary.emergency: If you are in immediate danger or cannot leave, call the emergency number for your country now and give your exact location and access needs.
boundary.privacy: Mindicraft does not request a precise location, infer or transmit your location, or store a survivor profile. You choose a country or region yourself to see the right official numbers.
not_included: live fire, road, evacuation-zone, shelter-capacity, or return-clearance data
fire prediction, route calculation, emergency dispatch, or missing-person matching
medical diagnosis, insurance or aid eligibility decisions, contractor recommendations, or guaranteed outcomes
accounts, precise-location collection, telemetry, donations, advertising, or public survivor posts

paths.title: I need to leave now
paths.summary: Leave first. Do not finish the page or try to protect property.

steps.text: If officials tell you to evacuate—or fire or smoke makes you feel unsafe—leave now. Do not stop to collect belongings or fight the fire.
Use the route officials name. Do not take shortcuts, cross a roadblock, or drive toward fire or downed power lines.
Only if they are close at hand, take people, medicines, medical or mobility equipment, phone and charger, identification, keys, and pets or service animals. Do not delay leaving.
If you cannot leave, call your local emergency number. Give your exact location and say if you need accessible transport, medical power, communication help, or animal support.
If it is safe and does not slow you down, tell one trusted person where you are going and who is with you.

paths.say: I am evacuating because of wildfire. I am at [location]. I need [transport, medical power, accessibility, language, or animal help]. Where should I go now?

paths.title: I am safely away and need help
paths.summary: Find a safe place for tonight, then handle one urgent need at a time.

steps.text: Use your local authority or recognized Red Cross or Red Crescent door to find an official shelter or evacuation centre. Confirm accessibility, service-animal, pet, and medical-power needs directly.
Ask first for injury care, medicines, safe water and food, accessible accommodation, charging or medical power, and help keeping your household together.
Do not return for belongings until local authorities reopen the area. Do not enter a fire-damaged building until the responsible authority or a qualified inspector says it can be entered.
When you have breathing room, keep identification, policy details, claim or aid numbers, receipts, photos, deadlines, and dated contact notes together in one recovery folder.
Open disaster aid through an official government or recognized humanitarian website. Eligibility, deadlines, shelter openings, and payment amounts change by event; this page does not promise them.

paths.say: I have evacuated because of wildfire. I need [shelter, medicine, accessible accommodation, food, charging, transport, or animal help] today. What official service can help me?

paths.title: Smoke is affecting me
paths.summary: Evacuation orders come first. Otherwise reduce smoke exposure and use health help when needed.

steps.text: Smoke advice is not permission to stay near a fire. If officials tell you to evacuate, leave immediately.

If there is no evacuation order and it is safe to remain indoors, move to cleaner, cooler indoor air; close windows and doors when safe, use recirculation and suitable filtration, and avoid making more indoor smoke or particles.

A well-fitting particulate respirator certified by the authority in your country—for example, a NIOSH-approved N95 or P100 in the United States—can reduce particle exposure. It does not supply oxygen, protect against gases, or replace evacuation.
Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, a serious asthma attack, marked dizziness, or a rapidly worsening condition needs urgent medical help through your local health or emergency system.
Children, older adults, pregnant people, and people with heart or lung conditions can face greater smoke risk. Use current local public-health advice for the person in front of you.

paths.say: Wildfire smoke is affecting my breathing or health. My symptoms are [plain description]. Where can I get urgent advice or cleaner air now?

paths.title: I may be returning home
paths.summary: Return only after authorities reopen the area, and enter a damaged building only after responsible clearance. Fire damage can hide heat, electricity, structural, water, and ash hazards.

steps.text: Return only after local authorities reopen the area. Enter a fire-damaged building only after the responsible authority or a qualified inspector says it is safe. A quiet street, map, or social post is not clearance.
Avoid hot ash, embers, unstable trees or buildings, downed lines, damaged tanks, batteries, and chemical containers. Do not restore utilities yourself.

Follow local public-health advice before using tap or private-well water, or food exposed to fire, ash, heat, damaged packaging, or lost refrigeration. Sealed, undamaged supplies from a safe source can still be used.
When it is safe, photograph or video damage before moving or discarding items. Contact the insurer or landlord and ask what urgent work or disposal they authorize.

Keep children, pets, older adults, and people with heart or lung conditions away from ash cleanup. Burned-structure ash may contain hazardous material; follow the local debris program before cleanup and use the protection it requires.

paths.say: Have local authorities reopened my area? Has the responsible authority or a qualified inspector cleared this damaged building for entry? What water, utility, ash, and structural restrictions still apply?

paths.title: I am starting recovery or rebuilding
paths.summary: Make one record, use official doors, and do not let urgency force an unsafe contract or payment.

steps.text: Contact the insurer or landlord through contact details you verify yourself. Ask about temporary housing, emergency work, evidence, disposal, deadlines, and the next named step.
Keep copies of forms, photos, receipts, claim and application numbers, names, dates, promises, deadlines, and decisions outside the damaged home or device.
Before hiring, verify the contractor through the local regulator, obtain written estimates and scope, and do not sign a blank document or pay the entire amount in advance.
Ask the local building authority which permits, debris rules, and current fire-resilient building requirements apply before reconstruction.

Safety, shelter, food, medication, trusted contact, and practical help come before retelling the event. Distress after an emergency is common; local health and crisis services can help when it is too much to carry alone.

paths.say: I am recovering from wildfire. My next need is [housing, documents, insurance, aid, cleanup, work, school, animals, or emotional support]. Which official service owns that step?

paths.title: I am helping someone
paths.summary: Offer calm practical help, preserve choice, and connect the person to current local services.

steps.text: Check immediate safety first. If the person is in danger, help them contact local emergency services or follow an evacuation order; do not send them back for belongings.
Ask what practical help they want now: transport, shelter, medication, charging, food, animal care, translation, paperwork, or simply someone trusted beside them.
Listen without pressing for details or asking them to retell the event. Respect dignity, culture, ability, privacy, and refusal.
Share the exact official page or number, say when you checked it, and be honest if shelter space, eligibility, hours, or response are unknown.
A useful message is: I see what is happening. You do not have to solve everything today. I can help with one practical thing you choose.

paths.say: I see what is happening. You do not have to explain it all. What is one practical thing you want help with right now?

support_needs.title: Accessible transport
support_needs.ask: I am evacuating because of wildfire. I need accessible transport and have [mobility, communication, medical, or service-animal need]. Where should I go now?

support_needs.title: Shelter tonight
support_needs.ask: I have evacuated because of wildfire. I need an official shelter for [people, children, service animal, pets] and need [accessibility or medical power]. What is open now?

support_needs.title: Medicine or medical power
support_needs.ask: I have been displaced by wildfire and need [medicine, refrigeration, charging, oxygen, or powered equipment]. Which health or shelter service can help today?

support_needs.title: Pets, service animals, or livestock
support_needs.ask: I am evacuating with [pet, service animal, or livestock]. Which official animal-safe shelter or local animal authority should I contact?

support_needs.title: Housing, money, or disaster aid
support_needs.ask: I was displaced or lost property in a wildfire. Which official program applies to this event in my area? Has it been formally declared, and does that affect eligibility or deadlines? What documents should I verify?

support_needs.title: Emotional support
support_needs.ask: I have been affected by wildfire and need confidential emotional support. Which local disaster or crisis service can I contact now?
